docs.title: Orchestrator · Risk Manager
docs.text:
A monitoring orchestrator: each cycle it reads account health and enforces guard rails — if drawdown or margin level breaches a limit, it closes everything (a kill-switch). Built entirely on MT5Sugar.

Source: examples/demos/orchestrators/14_risk_manager.cpp · Run: ./build/demos 14 · API level: HIGH (Sugar)

Read-only until a breach

Unlike the other orchestrators, this one opens nothing. It only monitors and, on a breach, flattens the book. Safe to run at any time.

docs.title: 🎯 What it does
docs.text:
1. Records the start balance.
  2. Each cycle reads equity, margin level, floating P/L and open-position count.
  3. Computes drawdown % = (startBalance − equity) / startBalance × 100.
  4. If drawdown > maxDrawdownPct, or (with positions open) margin level < minMarginLevel → closeAllPositions() and stop.

docs.title: 🧩 The pattern
docs.text:
RiskManager{config} → run(cycles):
    read equity / marginLevel / floatP&L / openCount → evaluate limits
    → breach? closeAllPositions + stop : wait → repeat

docs.title: ⚙️ Config
docs.text:
struct Config {
    double maxDrawdownPct{5.0};    // close all if equity is this % below the start balance
    double minMarginLevel{150.0};  // ... or if margin level drops below this % (with positions open)
    int    cycles{5};
    int    intervalMs{800};
};

docs.title: 🏗️ The orchestrator (annotated)
docs.text:
class RiskManager {
public:
    struct Config { double maxDrawdownPct{5.0}; double minMarginLevel{150.0};
                    int cycles{5}; int intervalMs{800}; };

    RiskManager(MT5Sugar& sugar, Config cfg) : m_s(sugar), m_cfg(cfg) {
        m_startBalance = sugar.getBalance();      // baseline for drawdown
    }

    void run() {
        for (int c = 1; c <= m_cfg.cycles; ++c) {
            double equity      = m_s.getEquity();
            double marginLevel = m_s.getMarginLevel();   // 0 when no margin is used
            double floating    = m_s.getTotalProfit();
            int    open        = m_s.countOpenPositions();
            double ddPct = m_startBalance > 0
                         ? (m_startBalance - equity) / m_startBalance * 100.0 : 0.0;

            bool breach = (ddPct > m_cfg.maxDrawdownPct) ||
                          (open > 0 && marginLevel > 0 && marginLevel < m_cfg.minMarginLevel);
            if (breach) {
                m_s.closeAllPositions();              // kill-switch
                break;
            }
            std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(m_cfg.intervalMs));
        }
    }
private:
    MT5Sugar& m_s; Config m_cfg; double m_startBalance{0};
};

Key Sugar calls: getBalance (baseline) · getEquity · getMarginLevel · getTotalProfit · countOpenPositions · closeAllPositions.

Why marginLevel > 0 in the check: a flat account reports 0% margin level — without that guard the kill-switch would fire the moment you have no positions.

docs.title: 1) Run it with defaults
docs.text:
MT5Sugar sugar("mt5.mrpc.pro", 443);
sugar.connect(5057947437, "password", "MetaQuotes-Demo");

RiskManager rm(sugar, RiskManager::Config{});
rm.run();   // monitors 5 cycles; flattens on a breach

docs.title: 2) Stricter limits, longer watch
docs.text:
RiskManager::Config cfg;
cfg.maxDrawdownPct = 2.0;     // very tight drawdown budget
cfg.minMarginLevel = 300.0;   // demand a comfortable cushion
cfg.cycles         = 60;      // watch for ~48 s at 800 ms
RiskManager(sugar, cfg).run();

docs.title: 3) Run the monitor on a background thread while you trade
docs.text:
#include <thread>
#include <atomic>

std::atomic<bool> stop{false};
std::thread guard([&]{
    double start = sugar.getBalance();
    while (!stop) {
        double dd = (start - sugar.getEquity()) / start * 100.0;
        bool open = sugar.countOpenPositions() > 0;
        double lvl = sugar.getMarginLevel();
        if (dd > 5.0 || (open && lvl > 0 && lvl < 150.0)) {
            sugar.closeAllPositions();
            break;
        }
        std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::seconds(1));
    }
});

// ... place and manage trades on the main thread ...

stop = true; guard.join();

docs.title: 4) Daily-loss kill-switch (realized + floating)
docs.text:
Combine floating P/L with today's realized loss for a hard daily cap:

double realizedToday = sugar.getProfitToday();     // closed trades
double floating      = sugar.getTotalProfit();     // open trades
if (realizedToday + floating < -200.0) {           // $200 daily stop
    sugar.closeAllPositions();
    std::puts("daily loss limit hit — flat for the day");
}

docs.title: 5) Report-only (no kill-switch)
docs.text:
Strip the action to get a pure health monitor:

void report(MT5Sugar& sugar) {
    std::printf("equity %.2f | marginLevel %.1f%% | floatP/L %.2f | open %d\n",
                sugar.getEquity(), sugar.getMarginLevel(),
                sugar.getTotalProfit(), sugar.countOpenPositions());
}

docs.title: ⚠️ Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Flat account = 0% margin level. Always guard the margin-level check with open > 0 && marginLevel > 0 (as the code does) or it misfires.
  • Baseline is the start balance, not equity — drawdown is measured from where you began the run.
  • Kill-switch is all-or-nothing. closeAllPositions() flattens everything; scope it (closeAllBySymbol) if you only manage one market.
  • Polling cadence. A 1 s loop reacts within a second; shorten intervalMs for faster protection at the cost of more calls.

docs.title: Orchestrator · Trailing Stop
docs.text:
Open one position, then ratchet its stop loss up as price advances — never down. The classic "let winners run, cap the downside" manager, built entirely on MT5Sugar.

Source: examples/demos/orchestrators/11_trailing_stop.cpp · Run: ./build/demos 11 · API level: HIGH (Sugar)

Educational example

Places a small live 0.01 BUY on the demo account and closes it before returning. The heuristic (a fixed pip trail) is a template to build on, not a turnkey system.

docs.title: 🎯 What it does
docs.text:
1. Opens a market BUY.
  2. Each cycle, reads the bid and computes a stop trailPips behind it.
  3. Raises the SL only if the new level is higher than the current one (monotonic ratchet).
  4. Closes the position at the end of the run.

docs.title: 🧩 The pattern
docs.text:
TrailingStop{config} → buyMarket → run(cycles):
    read bid → wantSL = bid - trailPips·pip → if wantSL > bestSL: raise SL → repeat
→ closePosition

docs.title: ⚙️ Config
docs.text:
struct Config {
    double trailPips{20.0};   // keep the SL this many pips behind the best bid
    int    cycles{8};         // how many times to re-evaluate
    int    intervalMs{700};   // pause between cycles
};

docs.title: 🏗️ The orchestrator (annotated)
docs.text:
class TrailingStop {
public:
    struct Config { double trailPips{20.0}; int cycles{8}; int intervalMs{700}; };

    TrailingStop(MT5Sugar& sugar, std::string symbol, double volume, Config cfg)
        : m_s(sugar), m_sym(std::move(symbol)), m_vol(volume), m_cfg(cfg) {
        // pip = point, scaled ×10 on 3/5-digit symbols (so "pips" means what a trader means)
        m_pip = sugar.getSymbolInfo(m_sym).point;
        int d = sugar.getSymbolDigits(m_sym);
        if (d == 3 || d == 5) m_pip *= 10.0;
    }

    void run() {
        uint64_t ticket = m_s.buyMarket(m_sym, m_vol);
        if (ticket == 0) return;                 // rejected (market closed?) — nothing to trail

        double bestSL = 0;
        for (int c = 1; c <= m_cfg.cycles; ++c) {
            std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(m_cfg.intervalMs));

            bool found = false;
            Position p = m_s.getPositionByTicket((int64_t)ticket, found);
            if (!found) return;                  // closed elsewhere — stop managing it

            double bid    = m_s.getBid(m_sym);
            double wantSL = bid - m_cfg.trailPips * m_pip;
            if (wantSL > bestSL) {               // only ever tighten
                bestSL = wantSL;
                m_s.modifyPositionSL((int64_t)ticket, bestSL);
            }
        }
        m_s.closePosition((int64_t)ticket);
    }
private:
    MT5Sugar& m_s; std::string m_sym; double m_vol, m_pip{0}; Config m_cfg;
};

Key Sugar calls: buyMarket · getSymbolInfo / getSymbolDigits (pip sizing) · getBid · getPositionByTicket · modifyPositionSL · closePosition.

docs.title: 1) Run it with defaults
docs.text:
MT5Sugar sugar("mt5.mrpc.pro", 443);
sugar.connect(5057947437, "password", "MetaQuotes-Demo");

TrailingStop ts(sugar, "EURUSD", 0.01, TrailingStop::Config{});
ts.run();   // opens, trails for 8 cycles, closes

docs.title: 2) A tighter, faster trail
docs.text:
TrailingStop::Config cfg;
cfg.trailPips  = 10;    // hug price closer
cfg.cycles     = 30;    // manage longer
cfg.intervalMs = 400;   // check more often
TrailingStop(sugar, "EURUSD", 0.02, cfg).run();

docs.title: 3) Trail an existing position instead of opening one
docs.text:
The demo opens its own trade; in a real strategy you often already hold one. The core is just the ratchet — apply it to any ticket:

void trailExisting(MT5Sugar& sugar, int64_t ticket, double trailPips, int cycles) {
    bool found = false;
    Position p0 = sugar.getPositionByTicket(ticket, found);
    if (!found) return;
    double pip = sugar.getSymbolInfo(p0.symbol).point;
    if (sugar.getSymbolDigits(p0.symbol) % 2 == 1) pip *= 10.0;   // 3/5-digit → ×10

    double bestSL = p0.stopLoss;
    for (int c = 0; c < cycles; ++c) {
        std::this_thread::sleep_for(std::chrono::milliseconds(500));
        bool ok = false; Position p = sugar.getPositionByTicket(ticket, ok);
        if (!ok) return;
        double wantSL = sugar.getBid(p.symbol) - trailPips * pip;
        if (wantSL > bestSL) { bestSL = wantSL; sugar.modifyPositionSL(ticket, bestSL); }
    }
}

docs.title: 4) Break-even first, then trail
docs.text:
Lock the stop at entry once in profit, then start trailing:

bool found = false;
Position p = sugar.getPositionByTicket(ticket, found);
double pip = sugar.getSymbolInfo(p.symbol).point * 10.0;   // 5-digit FX

if (found && sugar.getBid(p.symbol) > p.priceOpen + 10 * pip) {
    sugar.modifyPositionSL(ticket, p.priceOpen);            // break-even
    // ... then run the trail loop from example 3 ...
}

docs.title: 5) Respect the broker's minimum stop distance
docs.text:
A stop too close to price is rejected. Clamp the trail to getMinStopLevel:

double pip      = sugar.getSymbolInfo("EURUSD").point * 10.0;
double minDist  = sugar.getMinStopLevel("EURUSD") * sugar.getSymbolInfo("EURUSD").point;
double trail    = std::max(20 * pip, minDist);             // never closer than the broker allows
double wantSL   = sugar.getBid("EURUSD") - trail;

docs.title: ⚠️ Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Only raises the SL. By design it never loosens the stop — a reversal just hits the last locked level.
  • BUY-only demo. The example trails a long; for shorts, mirror it (getAsk, wantSL = ask + trail, only ever lower the SL).
  • Min stop distance. Too tight a trailPips → the modify is rejected (see example 5).
  • Position may vanish. getPositionByTicket(found=false) means it was closed elsewhere (TP hit, manual close) — the loop bails out cleanly.

docs.title: Adaptive Market-Mode Preset
docs.text:
A preset makes one decision and delegates the work to an orchestrator. The adaptive market-mode preset reads recent price action, classifies the market, and dispatches to the orchestrator that fits:

Market mode Chosen orchestrator Rationale TRENDING Trailing Stop ride the move, trail the stop RANGING Grid Trader fade the range with a pending grid VOLATILE Risk Manager defensive monitoring / kill-switch

Source: examples/demos/presets/16_adaptive_preset.cpp — run with ./build/demos 16.

docs.title: How it analyses the market
docs.text:
It pulls the last 20 H1 bars through MT5Service::lastBars and derives three cheap numbers:

auto bars = sugar.service().lastBars(symbol, Timeframe::H1, 20);

double sumRange = 0, maxRange = 0;
for (const auto& b : bars) { double r = b.high - b.low; sumRange += r; maxRange = std::max(maxRange, r); }
double avgRange = sumRange / bars.size();                 // typical bar size  → volatility
double move     = std::fabs(bars.back().close - bars.front().close);
double trend    = avgRange > 0 ? move / avgRange : 0;     // net move in "average ranges"
double spike    = avgRange > 0 ? maxRange / avgRange : 1; // biggest bar vs typical

docs.title: How it decides
docs.text:
if      (spike > 2.5) mode = VOLATILE;   // an outsized bar → something is happening, be defensive
else if (trend > 2.0) mode = TRENDING;   // price drifted several ranges in one direction
else                  mode = RANGING;    // quiet, mean-reverting

switch (mode) {
    case TRENDING: demo_trailing_stop(sugar, cfg); break;
    case RANGING:  demo_grid_trader(sugar, cfg);   break;
    case VOLATILE: demo_risk_manager(sugar, cfg);  break;
}

docs.title: Example run
docs.text:
analysed 20 H1 bars:  avgRange=0.0009075  netMove=0.0003 (0.33 ranges)  maxSpike=1.63x
→ market mode: RANGING  → dispatching orchestrator
   (Grid Trader places a grid, lists it, removes it)

docs.title: 1) Run it
docs.text:
MT5Sugar sugar("mt5.mrpc.pro", 443);
sugar.connect(5057947437, "password", "MetaQuotes-Demo");

AdaptiveMarketModePreset preset(sugar, "EURUSD");
preset.execute(cfg);   // analyse → classify → dispatch to one orchestrator

docs.title: 2) Tune the classifier window / thresholds
docs.text:
The analysis is a few lines — fork it for a different regime definition:

auto bars = sugar.service().lastBars("EURUSD", Timeframe::M15, 50);   // finer, more bars
// ... recompute avgRange / trend / spike, then use your own thresholds ...
if      (spike > 3.0) mode = VOLATILE;   // more tolerant of spikes
else if (trend > 1.5) mode = TRENDING;   // quicker to call a trend
else                  mode = RANGING;

docs.title: 3) Classify without trading (regime signal only)
docs.text:
Use the analysis as a signal you feed elsewhere, instead of dispatching:

AdaptiveMarketModePreset preset(sugar, "EURUSD");
MarketMode mode = preset.analyse();                 // just the classification
std::printf("regime: %s\n", name(mode));
// → route to your own logic, size differently per regime, etc.

Note

The thresholds (2.5 spike, 2.0 trend) and the H1/20-bar window are deliberately simple and meant to be tuned. The value of the preset is the shape: analyse → classify → dispatch — a clean place to plug in real indicators or an economic calendar.
